title: What is lock fairness in ReentrantLock, how does a fair (FIFO) lock prevent starvation, and what is the throughput trade-off of fair versus unfair mode?
keyPoints: Fair lock: new ReentrantLock(true) grants ownership in FIFO order to prevent starvation.
Unfair lock (default): new ReentrantLock() allows barging for higher throughput.
Fair handoff wakes the specific queued thread, incurring a context-switch cost.
Unfair barging lets a running thread grab the lock in the same CPU window, avoiding the wake cost.
tryLock() with no timeout always barges even on a fair lock; use timed tryLock for fairness.
synchronized is always unfair; use ReentrantLock(true) when fairness is required.
Default to unfair for performance; switch to fair only when starvation is a real, observed problem.

s1_definition.oneliner: Fair locks serve threads in FIFO order to prevent starvation but pay a wake-up cost that lowers throughput; unfair locks let threads barge in for higher throughput at the risk of long waits.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Fair mode** – `new ReentrantLock(true)`: grants ownership in FIFO order so the longest-waiting thread is served next.
- **Unfair mode** – `new ReentrantLock()` (default): allows barging, where a newly arriving thread may grab the lock ahead of queued threads.
- **Throughput trade-off** – unfair avoids the context-switch cost of waking a parked thread, delivering higher throughput under contention.
- **tryLock() subtlety** – with no timeout, `tryLock()` always barges even on a fair lock; use `tryLock(timeout, unit)` for fair behaviour.
- **synchronized** – always unfair; `ReentrantLock(true)` is the only JDK tool for fair mutual exclusion.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, a fair lock is a strict token queue: customers take a numbered token and are served in exact order. An unfair lock is a free-for-all at the counter: whoever is closest jumps in. The free-for-all serves more per hour but an unlucky customer could wait a very long time.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Fair Lock (FIFO):
  Queue: [A] ← [B] ← [C] ← new thread D
  Lock freed → A gets it (head of queue)
  D joins the tail, served last

  Unfair Lock (Barging):
  Queue: [A] ← [B] ← [C]
  Lock freed → D arrives and barges in
  D gets the lock immediately
  A, B, C continue waiting

  Throughput:
  Fair:   │▓▓▓▓░░▓▓▓▓░░▓▓▓▓│  context switch gaps
  Unfair: │▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓│  no gaps, higher throughput
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Lock fairness is a mode chosen at construction. Fair locks grant ownership in FIFO order to prevent starvation but pay a context-switch cost on every handoff. Unfair locks allow barging for higher throughput.

I default to unfair for performance and switch to fair only when a thread is genuinely being starved, as we observed with our audit thread at National Bank of India.

Remember one sentence: fair locks trade throughput for ordering to prevent starvation, unfair locks trade ordering for throughput, and I default to unfair unless starvation is a real, observed problem.
